content: {"summary":"To verify whether PostgreSQL is still presenting the old certificate, run an openssl s_client against the DB port and compare the serial number to the one in the on‑disk server.crt. The replica (auth-db-02) also maintains its own certificate and timer and must be reloaded in the same way. The April 2025 incident was caused by the renewal timer writing a new cert but PostgreSQL never being reloaded, so the old cert continued to be served.","likely_cause":"PostgreSQL was not reloaded after the certificate renewal, leaving the old certificate in use.","confidence":"high","claims":[{"text":"Compare the server‑presented certificate with the on‑disk file using openssl and check serial numbers","evidence_ids":["RB-024#2"],"quote":"Different serials mean the server is still on the old certificate."},{"text":"The replica needs its own certificate and must be reloaded just like the primary","evidence_ids":["RB-024#3"],"quote":"Yes. auth-db-02 has its own certificate and its own timer."},{"text":"In April 2025 the timer wrote a new cert but PostgreSQL never loaded it, causing the old cert to be served","evidence_ids":["RB-024#4"],"quote":"but nothing told Postgres to load it."}],"next_checks":["Run the openssl s_client command on auth-db-01 and auth-db-02 and compare serials to the files in /etc/postgresql/16/main/","Execute SELECT pg_reload_conf(); or systemctl reload postgresql@16-main on both primary and replica","Check systemd timer status with systemctl list-timers pg-cert-renew.timer and journalctl for recent runs","Verify that the replica’s certificate files are present, owned by postgres, mode 0600, and match the CA chain"]}
